# 05 One line can declare several edges

## Outcome

`A --> B --> C` declares two edges. `A & B --> C & D` declares four. `A-->B;` ends a statement.
Three spellings, one idea: a line is not necessarily one statement.

## Why this ticket exists

All three are pure parser work — no contract changes, no layout, no renderer — and all three are
ordinary in real Mermaid documents. Chaining especially: writing `A --> B --> C` instead of two
lines is the first thing an author reaches for.

They are one ticket because they are one change to the same place: how an edge line is read.
Splitting them would mean three workers each widening `EDGE_RE` and each having to preserve the
other two's widening.

Ticket 04b of board 3 deliberately **pinned chained edges as rejected**, with a test, so that
whoever widened it had to do so on purpose. That test is yours to update, and its reasoning is
worth reading first: reading two of three nodes and dropping the rest would draw a diagram nobody
wrote, which is worse than an honest refusal. Whatever you do must not have that failure mode.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `A --> B --> C` declares edges `A-B` and `B-C`, and declares all three nodes. Assert the
      edge ids, since the `${from}-${to}` convention is what `timeline:` and `linkStyle` address.
- [x] Chaining works at length: `A --> B --> C --> D` is three edges, not two. An off-by-one here
      is the likely bug and a two-link test cannot catch it.
- [x] `A & B --> C` declares `A-C` and `B-C`. `A --> B & C` declares `A-B` and `A-C`.
      `A & B --> C & D` declares four, in a stated order — pick the order Mermaid produces and say
      how you determined it.
- [x] `&` and chaining compose: `A & B --> C --> D`. State what that means and assert it.
- [x] `;` ends a statement, so `A-->B;` and `A-->B; B-->C;` both work, and a trailing `;` on any
      other statement kind does too. Check whether `;` is a *separator* or a *terminator* in
      Mermaid and match it.
- [x] The `:::` shorthand still works on every endpoint of a chained or `&` line — board 3 landed
      it on both endpoints of a two-node edge, and this ticket multiplies the endpoints.
      `A:::hot --> B --> C:::cold` must apply both.
- [x] Board 3's pin (`index.test.ts`, "still calls a chained `A --> B --> C` unrecognized") is
      updated, and your report calls it out as the intended reversal it is.
- [x] Every existing flowchart test passes otherwise. This widens what is accepted; nothing that
      parsed before may change meaning.
- [x] The corpus's `chained`, `multi-node &` and `semicolon` entries move to `supported`, each
      asserting the edges produced, not merely that it rendered. `rejected` down three.
